body: Cases: Novo Nordisk (GLP-1 pioneer; Europe's most valuable company June 2024, then -73% to below pre-Wegovy levels by Feb 2026), Eli Lilly (fast follower with a better molecule; first $1tn drugmaker Nov 2025, ~63% of US branded obesity scripts), Monster (created a category and kept it), Celsius (new sub-category, 60x then -73%), Tesla (EVs; 35x then -73%), Nvidia (AI compute; see case_study:nvidia). Pattern: (1) the up-move begins when demand visibly exceeds supply (Wegovy shortages 2021-23, Model 3 waitlists, Pepsi DSD shelf space) — the signal is scarcity; (2) peak valuation tends to coincide with peak scarcity, exactly when competitors and capacity are arriving; (3) the winner is the player with the best head-to-head data/product and manufacturing/distribution scale (Lilly's SURPASS-2 and capacity spend; Monster's distribution system), not the first mover; (4) price normalisation (US government drug-price deals, compounding, EV price cuts) compresses margins at the same time as share loss. Early warning for the incumbent: a public head-to-head trial or benchmark that shows a superior rival, and its own next-gen product underwhelming (CagriSema Dec 2024). Lesson: in a new category, re-underwrite on competitive data every year; scarcity premiums are temporary.

data.signal_down: superior rival data; own next-gen miss; price normalisation

title: Category creation (GLP-1-type): the pioneer does not automatically win

body: In the severe/poor cases reviewed, outside parties found the problem years before the regulator ruled on it, and the signals tended to arrive in this order. (1) Financing and structure: promoter pledges rising, ICDs or 'general purpose corporate loans' to opaque entities (RHFL to ADAG shells, SEBI 2024; DHFL's 'Bandra Book', SEBI 2025: ~Rs 14,040 cr; Fortis ICDs 2017-18), listed assets securing group debt (Zee, Jaypee), thin float after relisting (Ruchi/Patanjali 2020). (2) Credit market: rating downgrades, CP/NCD rollovers failing, lender 'fraud' tags (SBI on RCom 2025; PNB on Srei 2022), or forged no-default letters (Gensol, 2025). (3) Gatekeepers: auditor qualifications or resignations, delayed accounts (Byju's FY21 ~18 months late; Deloitte quit Jun-2023), independent directors leaving, a forensic auditor reporting non-cooperation (Rajesh Exports, per SEBI's 3-Jun-2026 interim order). (4) Bank regulator signals: RBI divergences and refusal of a CEO's term (Yes Bank 2016-18), RBI special audits (Srei), supersession. (5) Outsiders: whistleblowers (Videocon 2016), investigative media (Cobrapost on DHFL 2019), short sellers (Hindenburg on Adani 2023, Viceroy on Vedanta 2025). The short-seller claims were largely not upheld by SEBI in Adani's case, so on their own they are prompts for diligence, not verdicts. (6) Regulators and agencies act last: SEBI interim orders, then ED/CBI, often 2-7 years later. Counter-example: Infosys (2019 whistleblower allegations not substantiated after an independent probe; stock recovered). Process rule: any one of items 1-3 means a deeper check; two together means exit or don't enter.

data.sequence: financing -> credit market -> gatekeepers -> RBI -> outsiders -> regulators

title: How governance problems typically surface first in India (the order of signals)

body: Novy-Marx, 'The Other Side of Value: The Gross Profitability Premium' (Journal of Financial Economics 108(1), 2013; ~1,800 citations): gross profits divided by total assets predicts US returns about as strongly as book-to-market, 1963-2010. The value-weighted long-short spread is roughly 0.3% per month, and the effect is negatively correlated with value, so combining the two (cheap AND profitable) roughly doubles the Sharpe ratio of either alone. Asness, Frazzini and Pedersen, 'Quality Minus Junk' (Review of Accounting Studies 24, 2019; ~190 citations on S2 for the journal version, far more for the SSRN version) define quality as profitable, growing, safe (low leverage and volatility) and well-run (high payout). High-quality stocks earn significant risk-adjusted returns in the US (from 1957) and in 24 countries. Quality stocks are priced at a premium, but not a large enough one, so investors underpay for quality. Replicated: yes. Profitability is one of the factors HXZ found survives, it is in the Fama-French five-factor model, and our own Ken French computation shows RMW was the steadiest premium after 2007 (2.6% a year vs 2.7% before). India: Nifty200 Quality 30 and the IIMA data also show a quality premium, though shorter samples. Use for us: high ROCE with cash conversion is a base-rate tailwind, not merely a 'story', and the valuation discipline should be 'cheap relative to quality', not 'cheap on P/B'.
title: Profitability/quality premium: Novy-Marx gross profitability (2013) and AQR Quality-Minus-Junk (2019)
